video_title: How LA Is Becoming America's New Industrial Tech Hub | Odd Lots
gist: Live Odd Lots conversation with Chris Power (Hadrian) and Tom Mueller (Impulse Space, ex-SpaceX employee #1) argues US reindustrialization is a civilizational race against China's manufacturing-and-military production base, and details how their companies (autonomous 'software-first' factories, in-space logistics) and the broader LA/South Bay cluster are trying to close the gap.

insights.claim: Chris Power argues reserve-currency status has flipped roughly every 150 years (Netherlands to British Empire to America), always after the incumbent power let its industrial/manufacturing edge atrophy into a financialized, offshored economy.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: Frames US de-industrialization as a historically recurring, structural pattern rather than a recent policy failure -- implying reversal requires rebuilding industrial capacity, not just financial engineering.
insights.quote: if you track these things roughly every 150 years, the reserve currency of all changes.

insights.claim: Chris Power claims the US was effectively the 'China' of World War Two -- winning not through superior engineering (Germany had that) but through sheer industrial mass-production output and logistics, and only became rich afterward via the Bretton Woods system.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: Suggests military/industrial dominance today is decided by production volume, not just technical sophistication -- relevant to how investors should weight manufacturing scale-up plays vs. pure R&D bets.
insights.quote: We were China in World War two. We just out produced them. We had better logistics.

themes.theme: US-China Industrial and Military Production Gap

insights.claim: Chris Power states that in war-game simulations China produces roughly 2,600 ships versus about 6 for the US, and that US missile inventories would be exhausted within seven days of expending current warehouse stock in a conflict.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: A stark, quantified capacity gap that underpins the bull case for US defense-manufacturing scale-up companies (like Hadrian) and for reshoring/defense-industrial-base investment generally.
insights.quote: China produce 2600 ships and we produce six

insights.claim: Chris Power argues China has treated industrial policy as a national-security function since 1985 (subsidizing energy, labor, capital and using export tariffs strategically), while the US treated industrial policy like financial spreadsheet returns for hedge funds -- and this asymmetry, not lack of American engineering talent, is the root cause of the manufacturing gap.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: Reframes the competitiveness problem as a deliberate, decades-long state strategy on China's side -- implying US countermeasures need to be equally structural (subsidies, security framing) rather than one-off tariffs.
insights.quote: since 85, the Americas traded industrial policy like, uh, financial spreadsheet returns for hedge funds.

insights.claim: Chris Power says that even if he modeled his factory at 0% labor and energy cost, Chinese-imported components would still be roughly three times cheaper than parts made from raw materials sourced and machined in the United States for some commercial customers.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: Shows labor-cost tariffs/reshoring narratives are incomplete -- raw material and capital subsidies in China create a cost gap that pure automation or wage arbitrage can't close, meaning policy (not just tech) is required.
insights.quote: I can buy the raw material in the United States, and it's three times the cost of the component in imported from China for some of our commercial customers.

insights.claim: Chris Power cites Chinese consumer drones (DJI) as an example of dumping economics: components that cost roughly $60 to make are sold to American consumers for about $20, undercutting domestic drone manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: A concrete example investors can use to gauge why US drone/robotics startups struggle on price and why policy responses (bans, not just tariffs) target specific hardware categories like drones.
insights.quote: those things cost 60 bucks and they sell them to American consumers for 20 bucks.

themes.theme: AI and Robotics as a Civilizational Race

insights.claim: Chris Power argues that AI progress is now bottlenecked by the 'velocity of training data,' which in turn depends on physical deployment at scale -- i.e., mass manufacturing capacity has become a rate-limiter for AI/robotics advancement, not just compute or algorithms.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: A non-obvious thesis linking industrial manufacturing capacity directly to AI competitiveness -- suggests investors should view physical production scale-up as an AI infrastructure play, not a separate sector.
insights.quote: most of software, especially AI, is now determined on what is the velocity of your training data, which means physical deployment.

insights.claim: Chris Power explicitly rejects framing humanoid robot competition (e.g., Tesla Optimus vs. Google) as benign consumer-product rivalry, arguing it is a direct national-security/military capability race with existential stakes.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: Investors treating humanoid robotics purely as a consumer/industrial-automation TAM story may be missing the defense-strategic framing that's driving capital and policy attention to the sector.
insights.quote: No no no no no, they're going to kill you.

insights.claim: Tom Mueller lays out a three-part framework for viable general-purpose robots: dexterity (human-like hands), vision (he considers largely solved), and an AI 'brain' -- once combined, he expects human-plus-superhuman capability.
insights.speaker: Tom Mueller (Impulse Space founder)
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist investors can use to evaluate which robotics companies are closest to a viable general-purpose product -- vision is treated as solved, so dexterity and integrated AI control are the remaining bottlenecks.
insights.quote: Once those pieces all come together, You have the capability to be human plus super human.

insights.claim: Tom Mueller argues that building infrastructure on the Moon and eventually Mars will require armies of robots rather than large human workforces, because sustained human presence in those environments is too dangerous and expensive.
insights.speaker: Tom Mueller (Impulse Space founder)
insights.so_what: Signals that space-industrial investment theses should weight robotics/autonomy providers as heavily as launch and habitat companies for lunar/Mars resource extraction plays.
insights.quote: you want an army of robots to build on the moon and eventually Mars.

insights.claim: Tom Mueller says reading Nick Bostrom's 'Superintelligence' years ago (with Elon Musk) alarmed them about AGI risk, but the timeline futurists expected (decades out) compressed dramatically faster than predicted once large language models emerged from simple next-word-prediction training.
insights.speaker: Tom Mueller (Impulse Space founder)
insights.so_what: First-hand account from an early Musk collaborator that AGI-adjacent risk timelines caught even informed insiders off guard -- relevant color for AI-safety and AI-race investment narratives.
insights.quote: So it happened much sooner than we thought and we're not ready for it.

insights.claim: Chris Power says roughly 90% of what looks like 'advanced manufacturing' is actually humans either doing digital engineering at a desktop or manually operating an otherwise 'dumb' machine on the factory floor -- meaning the real product being built at Hadrian is software, not robots.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: Corrects a common investor misconception that advanced-manufacturing startups are primarily robotics/hardware plays -- the defensible IP and margin driver is software orchestration, closer to an enterprise-software business model.
insights.quote: that's 90% of advanced manufacturing.

insights.claim: Hadrian positions itself as an automated contract manufacturer ('Foxconn to every defense problem') whose output ranges from individual spaceflight components to entire missiles to roughly 30% of the parts on a submarine build.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: Shows Hadrian's revenue exposure spans multiple high-value defense primes' supply chains simultaneously, making it a broad proxy for US defense-industrial-base re-shoring rather than a single-customer bet.
insights.quote: entire missile to 30% of a junior class submarine.

insights.claim: Chris Power explains that skilled machinists/welders must physically stand at machines not because the task requires a robot's dexterity, but because they are running real-time mental 'trigonometry' to predict tool wear/failure -- a problem he says is solvable with software (closing the control loop), not robotics.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: A specific, testable claim about where automation value actually accrues in manufacturing -- useful for evaluating competing automation startups that are betting on humanoid robots vs. closed-loop software.
insights.quote: They're genuinely doing trigonometry in their head, being like, oh, I think the tools are about to break and therefore I have to like stand in front of it.

insights.claim: Chris Power's rule of thumb is that every hardware company should keep about 10-15% of production in-house for the highest-risk, highest-skill 'hot pot' tasks, while scaling the rest through external suppliers.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: A concrete heuristic investors can apply when assessing whether a hardware startup's in-house/outsource mix is appropriately balanced for schedule risk vs. capital efficiency.
insights.quote: I agree, I think every company should have 10 to 15% in-house.

insights.claim: Tom Mueller describes a standard playbook at both SpaceX and Impulse Space: build the first development units of an engine or spacecraft entirely in-house to learn every failure mode in machining and assembly, then shift production to outside suppliers once the design is mature -- noting even SpaceX now sends some Raptor engine parts to outside shops like Hadrian.
insights.speaker: Tom Mueller (Impulse Space founder)
insights.so_what: Confirms even the most vertically integrated aerospace company (SpaceX) is now outsourcing mature production work to contract manufacturers like Hadrian -- a validating data point for the contract-manufacturing thesis.
insights.quote: you make your first development engine or spacecraft, you build it yourself and you learn all of the problems that you can have assembling it as machining it.

insights.claim: Chris Power says Hadrian's make-vs-buy decisions are driven primarily by trust in a supplier's ability to hit schedule, not by cost -- describing a case where he chose to spend $2 million on in-house CapEx rather than risk a legacy casting facility that could jeopardize a submarine program's timeline.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: Highlights schedule risk (not unit cost) as the dominant variable in defense-manufacturing sourcing decisions -- relevant for evaluating legacy suppliers' vulnerability to being displaced by newer, more reliable entrants.
insights.quote: I think in manufacturing you sell and buy trust.

insights.claim: Tom Mueller notes aerospace employment in the South Bay began climbing roughly 3-4 years after SpaceX's founding in 2002, and the area now hosts a dense cluster spanning nuclear, drone, defense and 3D-printing startups in addition to space companies -- summarized as 'software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware is done in LA.'
insights.speaker: Tom Mueller (Impulse Space founder)
insights.so_what: Identifies LA/South Bay as an emerging hardware-startup cluster analogous to Silicon Valley for software -- a regional thesis for where to look for the next wave of industrial-tech venture activity.
insights.quote: software is done in, in Silicon Valley, hardware is done in LA.

insights.claim: Tom Mueller says his own company and Hadrian both compete for and poach talent from each other as well as from legacy primes located nearby, such as Northrop Grumman (formerly TRW, where he worked 15 years) and Boeing.
insights.speaker: Tom Mueller (Impulse Space founder)
insights.so_what: Suggests a talent flywheel is forming where new industrial-tech startups are draining engineering talent from legacy defense primes -- a leading indicator of where innovation (and margin pressure on incumbents) is headed.
insights.quote: we're stealing talent from each other, certainly.

insights.claim: Chris Power argues blanket China tariffs are undermined in practice by transshipment loopholes (Chinese goods routed and relabeled through third countries like Singapore) and by ambiguous rules around what counts as 'assembly,' which can penalize legitimate US businesses importing partially assembled goods from Mexico.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: A specific mechanism explaining why headline tariff policy underperforms its intent -- useful for investors modeling the real-world effectiveness of reshoring/tariff-driven investment theses.
insights.quote: some Chinese company will ship something to Singapore. They'll call it Singapore.

insights.claim: Chris Power argues the more effective policy tool than broad tariffs is outright banning specific sensitive Chinese components (e.g., circuit boards in police/military drones and robots) even if it forces prices several times higher, because it channels the American consumer -- which he calls a bigger capital allocator than Blackstone or Blackrock -- toward domestic and allied supply chains.
insights.speaker: Chris Power (Hadrian founder)
insights.so_what: Suggests investors should watch for targeted component-level bans (not just tariffs) as the more durable policy lever reshaping supply chains in drones/robotics -- a specific regulatory catalyst to track.
insights.quote: the banning of components and assemblies to say, you've got to buy American American allies and let the market correct for cost is correct.

insights.claim: Tom Mueller recounts that when Elon Musk proposed catching the Starship booster with the launch tower's 'chopsticks' instead of landing legs, veteran engineers internally doubted it was possible -- yet it was successfully executed, reinforcing his takeaway that at SpaceX 'if it's possible, it's solvable.'
insights.speaker: Tom Mueller (Impulse Space founder)
insights.so_what: First-hand validation from SpaceX's first employee of Musk's track record of forcing through engineering solutions colleagues considered impossible -- relevant context for assessing execution risk on his other ventures.
insights.quote: And it's like, if it's possible, it's solvable.
